title: No School Will Decide Najya Hannah-Jones’s Future or Fate
author: Freddie deBoer
summary: Freddie deBoer argues that the Hannah-Jones controversy shows why historical perspective matters in education debates. He first dismisses the victory laps of school-choice advocates: one child in the unrepresentative New York City system is an anecdote, and the average American public school is doing fine, with problems concentrated in the poorest communities. He then lists the distinctly modern assumptions behind the debate, including the belief that student outcomes are highly mutable and determined mainly by schools. The decline of well-paid non-college work, he contends, explains why educational anxiety became acute after the Reagan era, and he describes a public school doom loop in which selective exit worsens public school metrics. His conclusion is that the debate keeps circling because neither liberals nor conservatives will admit that academic talent is unequally distributed, and he ends with what he hopes to teach his own son about love, luck, and adaptation.
points: DeBoer argues that New York City's size, demographics, and costs make it a poor basis for conclusions about American public schools.
He contends the average American public school is doing fine, with severe problems concentrated in a small number of disadvantaged schools.
The educational crisis narrative, he argues, intensified after offshoring and automation destroyed well-paid non-college jobs.
A public school doom loop forms when families of means leave and metrics fall further, fueling the narrative of public school inferiority.
His core claim is that unequal natural talent is forbidden knowledge in education debates, leaving policy stuck in the same circles.
quotes: Most obviously and importantly, this story is the definition of anecdote - it is, at best, a single data point about one particular child in one school system in one city.

But the reality is that our schooling problems are problems that afflict our poorest students in our most dysfunctional communities. If you are a middle class parent in a middle class city with schools filled with middle class kids, the odds are very good that your kid’s school is fine, and fine is all you need.

Because every particular about the debate over Hannah-Jones’s essay stems from a set of assumptions about what school is and does and is for, a set of assumptions that is profoundly modern and would largely appear foreign to most human beings for most of history.

As I’ve long argued, it’s no coincidence that the educational crisis narrative begins in the Reagan administration; the need to educate our citizenry into affluence became acute only after the alternative to education was destroyed.

And the reason why is because the most natural, obvious observation about human talents and abilities I can imagine - that they are unequally and unfairly distributed - is forbidden knowledge, something that most people know intuitively but feel they can never say.

What I can do is raise him to feel loved and valued, give him room to explore what he’s good at and what he likes doing, and constantly remind him that the greatest thing in life is to be a kind person and a loyal friend.
What would I tell Najya Hannah-Jones? I guess I would say, “Najya, your part is to be what you’ll be.
